title: Logical CCZ state cultivation
abstract: Logical CCZ states enable Toffoli gates, a central building block of fault-tolerant quantum arithmetic. We introduce an end-to-end protocol for direct CCZ-state preparation on bivariate tricycle and bicycle (BT/BB) codes. Our factory combines the cup-product CCZ gates native to BT codes with two novel ingredients, both enabled by engineering the logical coupling between BT and BB codes through projection-preserving lifts. Index-2 lifted BB ancillas enable selective $Z$-basis initialization, allowing the native cup-product gates to directly prepare two disjoint logical CCZ states. The prepared CCZ states are faithfully transferred to index-3 lifted BB memories with high code distance. We use decoder-based postselection to obtain high-fidelity output states with low overhead. We perform exact simulations of our factory under a circuit-level noise model motivated by neutral-atom hardware, obtaining joint infidelities of $1.84\times10^{-5}$ at $21.94\%$ acceptance and $4.10\times10^{-7}$ at $8.89\%$ acceptance for single-qubit, CZ, and CCZ error rates of $0.01\%$, $0.1\%$, and $0.5\%$, respectively. At the output-infidelity target of our smallest factory, its estimated spacetime cost per CCZ state is lower than that of $T$-state cultivation followed by CCZ conversion, providing an efficient route to logical CCZ states for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
summary: This paper presents a novel, end-to-end protocol for generating logical CCZ states required for fault-tolerant quantum arithmetic. It utilizes a combination of bivariate tricycle and bicycle quantum error correcting codes to achieve this preparation efficiently. The simulation results show low error rates and a reduced resource cost compared to alternative state preparation routes.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for an efficient, end-to-end protocol to directly prepare logical CCZ states, which are essential resources for implementing Toffoli gates in fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_result: They developed a factory using BT/BB codes that achieves low joint infidelities in simulations and demonstrates a lower estimated spacetime cost per CCZ state compared to established T-state conversion methods.
method: The protocol involves selective initialization using index-2 lifted BB codes, generating CCZ states via native cup-product gates, and then transferring these states to higher-distance BB memories using index-3 lifts, all enhanced by decoder-based postselection.
model_or_system: The work is based on quantum error correcting codes, specifically utilizing bivariate tricycle (BT) and bicycle (BB) codes, and engineering the logical coupling between them via projection-preserving lifts.
key_observables: Joint infidelities (e.g., $1.84 	imes 10^{-5}$), acceptance rates (e.g., 21.94%), and the estimated spacetime cost per CCZ state.
important_parameters: Error rates for single-qubit, CZ, and CCZ gates (0.01%, 0.1%, 0.5%); code distances ($d_f=3, 4, 5$).
main_assumptions: The protocol relies on the feasibility of projection-preserving lifts and uses decoder-based postselection to manage errors.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the three-step process: selective initialization of BT blocks, direct CCZ state generation via cup-product, and subsequent teleportation/escape into higher-distance BB blocks.
paper_structure: The paper details the protocol by first outlining the necessity of CCZ states, then describing the use of BT/BB codes for initialization and generation, followed by state transfer to higher-distance memories, and concluding with simulation results comparing its efficiency to T-state conversion.
why_interesting: The direct, resource-efficient cultivation of non-Clifford logical gates like CCZ is a major bottleneck in scaling quantum computation, making this protocol highly relevant for theorists designing fault-tolerant architectures.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Protocol overview. (a) Three BT blocks are selectively initialized in 0 + + , +0+ , and + + 0 using homomorphic measurements with index-2 lifted BB codes. (b) A depth-two cup-product circuit acting on the properly initialized BT states directly generates two disjoint logical CCZ states. (c) Homomorphic CNOTs subsequently teleport these states into three higher-distance BB blocks constructed through index-3 lifts.

FIG. 2. Lifting-based mechanisms. The coupling among the BT code QABC • , the BB code QAB • , and the lifted BB code eQAB • is illustrated. (a) Physical coupling of the three codes. We use the shorthand notation eQij = e Ai ⊗eBj, Qij = Ai ⊗Bj, and Qijk = Ai ⊗Bj ⊗Ck. The projection p maps the ν sheets of the lifted BB code eQAB • onto the base BB code QAB • . The inclusion ι embeds its two qubit sectors into the Q100 and Q010 sectors of the BT code QABC • . Their composition f = ι ◦p specifies the homomorphic CNOT. (b) Induced logical couplings. FIG. 3. Escape code memory error rate. We perform memory experiments under our noise model in both the X- basis and the Z-basis. The logical error rate per cycle is shown for the three BB codes used for escape. For J162, 2, 18K (X), no logical failure is observed at p = 2×10−3 among 108 shots, and the unfilled marker shows one-sided 95% upper limits.

FIG. 4. CCZ factory pipeline. (1) The BT and BB codes are initialized in the logical + and 0 states, respectively. (2) A homomorphic CNOT is applied with physical depth two. (3) The BB code is measured transversally in the Z basis; the outcomes are decoded, and adaptive feedback is applied. (4) The cup-product CCZ gate is applied to the three separately prepared BT code blocks. (5) The escape BB code is prepared in the logical 0 state. (6) A homomorphic CNOT is applied with physical depth three. (7) The BT code block is measured transversally in the X basis; the outcomes are decoded, and feedback is applied. FIG. 5. Joint decoding. Homomorphic CNOTs mix the stabilizer values of the three code blocks, so decoding should be performed jointly. The dotted lines show which measure- ment outcomes are jointly decoded. The outcomes supplied to decoder (B) are re-decoded using the output of decoder (C), as indicated by the green arrow.
